title: The Hawk and the Pigeons
summary: High in the peaceful rafters of a rustic farm dovecote, a flock of white pigeons lived in constant dread. Through unexpected trial and turning point, each character learns that inviting a tyrant to protect you from a petty foe invites your own slaughter.
full_text: High in the peaceful rafters of a rustic farm dovecote, a flock of white pigeons lived in constant dread. A fierce brown kite circled the skies above every afternoon, swooping down whenever a bird ventured into the open fields to forage for seeds. Though the kite managed to seize only a stray bird every few weeks, the pigeons lived in endless terror, shivering within the eaves and holding anxious assemblies to debate how they might secure their safety. In their desperation, an elder dove proposed a bold measure: 'Let us appeal to the great hawk, the undisputed master of the high winds! He possesses mighty talons and terrifying speed; if we invite him into our dovecote to serve as our royal protector, the cowardly kite will never dare show his face in our valley again.' Blinded by fear, the flock hailed the suggestion with enthusiasm. They sent an emissary to the hawk’s mountain aerie, promising him an honored dwelling in their roost. Flattered and hungry, the fierce hawk eagerly accepted their petition and flew down into the dovecote with an imposing display of sharp talons. No sooner was the hawk securely lodged within the narrow entrance of the roost than his predatory nature showed itself in all its fury. Barring the exit with his wide wings, he began slaughtering the helpless pigeons one by one, feasting upon more birds in a single morning than the kite had captured in an entire year! As the surviving pigeons huddled in the shadowy corners awaiting their doom, a dying dove wept in bitter remorse: 'Alas for our blind folly! In our eagerness to escape a minor annoyance, we have invited our greatest destroyer into our very home.' Too late did they learn that seeking the protection of a tyrant is a cure far deadlier than the affliction.
moral: Inviting a tyrant to protect you from a petty foe invites your own slaughter.

quiz.question: In the fable "The Hawk and the Pigeons", what situation triggers the main conflict?
options: A confrontation arising from conflicting desires, needs, or natural traits
A sudden storm that drove all animals far across the open plains
A royal decree ordering all beasts to leave the countryside
A festival where the creatures exchanged gifts in harmony
quiz.hint: Recall the events that begin the story.

quiz.question: What critical action or realization changes the course of the story?
options: One character's true nature or limits are revealed through their actions
An outside judge arrives to solve the problem for both parties
Both characters agree to forget what happened and walk away
The smaller character suddenly transforms into a giant beast
quiz.hint: Think about how the conflict reaches its resolution.

quiz.question: What essential truth does "The Hawk and the Pigeons" teach young readers?
options: Inviting a tyrant to protect you from a petty foe invites your own slaughter.
Might and physical strength always triumph over truth and wisdom
Flattery is the safest and most honest way to make lifelong friends
It is wise to pretend to be someone you are not in times of trouble
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the final moral lesson of the fable.

discussion_questions.prompt: Who are the central characters in "The Hawk and the Pigeons", and what was each trying to accomplish at the beginning?
Why does this fable conclude with the moral that "Inviting a tyrant to protect you from a petty foe invites your own slaughter"? How do the characters' choices illustrate this?
Think of a situation at school, sports, or home where someone might face a similar dilemma. How can you apply this lesson?
Were the consequences faced by the characters fair? What alternative choice could have produced a wiser outcome?
Imagine if the characters met again one year later. How would their behavior change based on what they learned today?
